Sunday, 10:40 pm
Parveen: she took my phone and said no trip 😠 I'm not a baby!!
Lalit: What happened?
Parveen: I came home at 9 and didn't tell her. She acts like I'm a criminal. She NEVER listens
Lalit: Ok. Want to talk tomorrow?
Parveen: whatever

Monday, 7:15 am
Parveen: ok so mum was sitting at the door when I got home last night
Parveen: I didn't see it then. She'd called me like 12 times, my phone was on silent
Parveen: she said the auto stand near our lane was closed and she pictured me alone at the bus stop
Lalit: So she was scared?
Parveen: yeah 😔 I still think she overreacted. But I get it. I'm going to say sorry for the silent phone

qa.q: How many times had Parveen's mum called Parveen the night before?
qa.a: She had called about 12 times.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling at 10:40 on Sunday night?
qa.a: Parveen was angry and felt misunderstood, as the angry face, "I'm not a baby" and "She NEVER listens" show.

qa.q: What choice did Parveen make that turned the quarrel toward repair?
qa.a: After sleeping on it, Parveen chose to apologise for the silent phone, without giving up the view that Mum overreacted. Waiting let Parveen see the other side.

qa.q: What was Parveen's mum feeling that evening, according to Parveen?
qa.a: She was frightened. She sat waiting at the door and pictured Parveen alone at a bus stop. 🤍

grounding: A teenager quarrelling with a parent sees only one side until, calmer the next morning, the parent's fear becomes clear.

passage:
Manjula slammed the gate so hard the hens scattered. "You don't trust me!" she had shouted, and her father Kunal had said only, "You are not riding to college on the highway after dark, and that's final." In her head, the reasons piled up: every other girl in the village did it, he treated her like glass, he never listened.
She sat on the roof with her arms crossed until the light went orange. Slowly the hot feeling drained out. She remembered last monsoon, when the bus was late and she came off it at eight to find Kunal standing at the stop with a torch and his slippers wet through, saying nothing, just walking beside her home.
That night she carried his tea to the cot. "Baba, I was angry," she said. "Can we talk about the college timings again?"

qa.q: What did Kunal say he would not allow?
qa.a: He said she was not to ride to college on the highway after dark.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling on the roof, and how did it change?
qa.a: She was hot with anger at first, then it drained away. Remembering the torch and wet slippers at the bus stop softened her, and she felt ready to talk.

qa.q: What helped Manjula move from shouting to talking?
qa.a: She waited on the roof until her anger drained, then remembered his waiting for her. Then she asked to talk about the timings and did not restart the fight.

qa.q: How does Kunal probably see Manjula's shouting and slammed gate?
qa.a: He may see it as hurtful, yet still as a young person's frustration. His rule comes from fear, and calm talk later gives him room to listen to her.

grounding: A teenager quarrelling with her father sees only her side until calm returns and she recalls his fear for her.

passage: The hostel phone booth at Sunbeam Residential School had a queue, and Zainab didn't care who heard. "Abbu, everyone is going on the trek! It's two days! You never let me do anything!" Her father's voice was small through the old receiver. "I said no, Zainab. Not the hills." She slammed the phone down, and the warden, Mrs. Thomas, raised an eyebrow. Zainab stormed off to the common room, fuming, and sat next to Gautam, who was doing sums. "He treats me like a baby." Gautam didn't answer. An hour later, after dinner, the knot in her chest had loosened. She remembered, suddenly, that Abbu's younger brother had slipped on a hill path years ago and never walked properly again. She went back to the booth. "Abbu, is it because of Chachu?" There was a long pause. "Yes, beta."

qa.q: What trip did Zainab want to go on?
qa.a: She wanted to go on a two-day trek with everyone.

qa.q: How did Zainab's feelings change between the call and after dinner?
qa.a: At first she was furious and felt treated like a baby; after dinner, once she was calmer, she felt ready to understand Abbu's fear.

qa.q: What could Zainab do next time a quarrel with Abbu flares up?
qa.a: She could say she needs some time, end the call calmly, and call back once she has cooled down, instead of slamming the phone.

qa.q: How might Abbu have seen the trek?
qa.a: Because his younger brother was hurt on a hill path, Abbu probably felt frightened for Zainab, not controlling, and the word 'hills' carried that memory.

grounding: Shows a teenager who can see only her side while quarrelling, and who understands her father's fear once she has calmed down.

passage:
Amma,

I'm writing this because every time I try to say it out loud, we both start shouting again.

Last night, when you took my phone after I came home at eleven from Zainab's birthday, I thought you were the most unfair person alive. I said things I shouldn't have. In that moment all I could see was how embarrassed I felt in front of Zainab's mother, and how you "never trust me."

This morning, lying awake, I remembered you standing at the gate in your nightie. You'd called me seven times. My phone was on silent. I think you were scared something had happened to me.

I'm still a bit annoyed about the phone. But I get it now, more than I did at eleven o'clock.

Your daughter,
Ganga

qa.q: What time did Ganga come home from Zainab's birthday?
qa.a: Ganga came home at eleven.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling during the quarrel the night before?
qa.a: Ganga felt angry and embarrassed in front of Zainab's mother, and convinced that Amma was being unfair and did not trust her.

qa.q: What would you advise Ganga and her mother for the next disagreement?
qa.a: Pause the argument and talk the next morning, as Ganga did in the letter, and agree on a simple check-in text when plans run late.

qa.q: What was it like for Amma waiting at the gate?
qa.a: Amma had called seven times with no answer, so she was probably frightened that something had happened to Ganga.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, calm the next morning, understands the fear behind her mother's anger that she could not see during the quarrel.

passage:
"Avni, don't laugh, okay? Last night I had the biggest fight with Papa. Like, door-slamming level.
So the district match was in Pune, and the team was going by night bus, and he said, "Manoj, no." Just no. I said he doesn't care about my cricket, he only cares about marks. I said he's jealous because he never got to play. I actually said that.
Then I went to my room and put my headphones on and felt totally right. For like an hour.
And then Mummy came in and told me Papa had been reading about night bus accidents on the highway all week. He'd even called the coach twice.
Avni, I felt so stupid. I still wanted to go! But I think I could only see my side because I was so angry. This morning I said sorry, and I'm going to ask if he'll drive me instead."

qa.q: How was the team travelling to the district match in Pune?
qa.a: The team was going by night bus.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after hearing what Papa had been reading?
qa.a: Manoj felt foolish and ashamed of those words, while still wanting to go to the match.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying sorry in the morning and offering the drive as another way worked, because it respects Papa's fear and still gives Manoj a way to play.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had waited to talk until he was calm?
qa.a: Manoj might not have said hurtful things like calling Papa jealous, and could have asked what was worrying Papa before the fight grew.

grounding: Shows a teenager so angry during a quarrel that only one side is visible, who later understands Papa's fear once calm.

passage:
Friday. "You never trust me!" Noor shouted, and slammed her door. Abbu's voice came through it: "The party ends at eleven, and that flyover road has no lights—" She didn't hear the rest. All she heard was no. Divyansh's whole class would be there, and she would be the only one missing.
Sunday. Noor woke early and found Abbu asleep in his chair by the window, still in his office shirt, his phone on his chest. Ammi said quietly, "He waited up to see if you'd go anyway."
Tuesday. Noor sat beside him on the balcony. "You weren't saying no to me. You were scared of the road." Abbu let out a long breath. "Very scared." They agreed: next time, he would drive her and pick her up by ten-thirty.

qa.q: What time did Divyansh's party end?
qa.a: The party ended at eleven.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling on Friday night?
qa.a: Noor felt angry and hurt, sure that Abbu did not trust her, so she heard only the no.

qa.q: What could Noor try the next time a quarrel heats up?
qa.a: She could say she needs a break and come back to it the next day, when she can hear the reasons as well as the no.

qa.q: How did Abbu see the party request?
qa.a: He was afraid of Noor travelling home late on the dark flyover road, so his no came from fear, not distrust.

grounding: Shows a teenager who can see only her own side while quarrelling with her father, and who understands his fear once she has calmed down.
